    A Michelin Plate stall and Chomp Chomp's most famous name — thick yellow noodles and bee hoon fried with prawns and squid in a prawn stock simmered for hours, finished with a dollop of sambal. The go-to plate at Serangoon Gardens' legendary supper hawker centre.

    Chomp Chomp Food Centre, 20 Kensington Park Road, S557269

  2. 2 Must see within Upper Serangoon · Chinese

    Ming Fa Duck Rice

    One of Singapore's best Teochew braised duck rice stalls, tucked in Hougang's Hainanese Village Centre (Lorong Ah Soo). Tender lean duck over yam rice, drenched in a mildly sweet-savoury five-spice sauce, with an anchovy-loaded sambal. Opens at dawn and usually sells out by early lunch.

    Hainanese Village Centre, 105 Hougang Avenue 1, #02-01, Singapore 530105

  3. 3 Must see within Upper Serangoon · Wok Noodles

    Hougang Oyster Omelette & Fried Kway Teow

    A 30-year Hougang heritage stall run by Mr and Mrs Ong that still fries its oyster omelette in pork lard, with big juicy oysters and a fragrant char kway teow alongside. One of the island's best-rated orh luak, worth the queue.

  4. 4 Must see within Upper Serangoon

    Hougang Tou Mu Kung (Kew Ong Yah Temple)

    Singapore's oldest temple dedicated to the Nine Emperor Gods (Kew Ong Yah), completed 1921 and gazetted a National Monument on 14 Jan 2005. Its blend of Hokkien and later Teochew roof forms anchors Hougang's Teochew heritage, and it remains the focus of the annual Nine Emperor Gods Festival.

    Look for Free entry; busiest during the ninth-lunar-month festival

    779A Upper Serangoon Road, Singapore

    Recommended by , ,

  5. 5 Must see within Upper Serangoon

    Kampong Lorong Buangkok

    Singapore's last surviving mainland village, established in 1956 when traditional-medicine seller Sng Teow Koon bought the swampy land and rented plots to Malay and Chinese families. A cluster of zinc-roofed houses on dirt tracks around a surau, in the Trafalgar (Buangkok) subzone of Hougang; Ms Sng Mui Hong, the founder's youngest daughter, still lives here as landlord. Old four-digit street signs survive.

    Look for Free; a living village — visit respectfully, don't enter homes

    7 Lorong Buangkok (off Gerald Drive, via Buangkok Crescent), Singapore 547557

    Recommended by , ,

  10. 10 Must see within Upper Serangoon

    Church of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary

    A National Monument (gazetted 14 Jan 2005) and the historic heart of Serangoon's Teochew Catholic community, which was mostly farmers in the 19th century. The present Gothic church — pointed arches, a soaring nave — was blessed on 8 Dec 1901 and restored in 2019; the mission dates to pioneer priest Fr Ambrose Maistre in 1852.

    Look for Free entry; a stop on the Hougang Heritage Trail

    1259 Upper Serangoon Road, Singapore 534795

    Recommended by ,

    Chomp Chomp Food Centre

    Serangoon Gardens' legendary supper hawker centre, open since 1972 with around 36 stalls. A night-time institution for BBQ stingray and sotong, Hokkien mee, satay, satay bee hoon, orh luak and charcoal chicken wings — as much a neighbourhood landmark as an eating spot.

    Look for Evenings to late night; busiest for supper

    20 Kensington Park Road, Singapore 557269

  14. 14 Worth the detour within Upper Serangoon

    Chee Tong Temple

    Completed in 1987 and designed by Tay Kheng Soon of Akitek Tenggara, this is widely regarded as Singapore's first truly modernist Chinese temple — its roof rising in eight-sided prisms that evoke a lotus, its corners deliberately kept un-sharp on the deities' guidance. A Hougang Heritage Trail 'Architectural Gem' and a documented modern-movement building.

    Look for Active temple; open daytime

    62 Hougang Avenue 3, Singapore 538844

    Recommended by , ,

  33. 33 Worth the detour within Upper Serangoon

    Serangoon Garden Estate & Circus

    One of Singapore's oldest private landed estates, laid out in the 1950s by British developer Steven Charles Macey to house British, Australian and NZ servicemen from the nearby RAF Chia Keng camp — which is why nearly every street bears a British name. The Circus roundabout is its social heart, ringed by Chomp Chomp, the market and myVillage.

    Look for Residential estate; open streetscape

    Serangoon Garden Circus (Serangoon Garden Way / Kensington Park Road), Singapore

    Recommended by ,

  34. 34 Worth the detour within Upper Serangoon

    Hougang Heritage Trail

    NHB's self-guided trail through 'Au Kang' — one of Singapore's oldest heartland towns and a historic Teochew enclave. Eighteen sites across three routes ('Landmarks of Hougang', 'Institutions of Service', 'Architectural Gems'), and the first heartland trail to include two National Monuments (Church of the Nativity and Tou Mu Kung).

    Look for Free; booklet & map on Roots.gov.sg

    Upper Serangoon Road (trail markers near Kovan MRT), Singapore

    Recommended by ,

    Punggol Park

    A 16-hectare Hougang park built around a 5-hectare lake — a former sand quarry once used to reclaim the area's swamps. Popular for lakeside jogging, fishing decks and a heron-frequented waterfront, and a green anchor of the Hougang edge.

    Look for Open 24h, free

    Hougang Avenue 8 (junction of Hougang Ave 8 & Ave 10), Singapore

    The oldest mosque in Hougang, built in 1921 on land donated by Gujarati merchant-philanthropist Ahmad Mohamed Salleh Angullia to serve the area's Muslim community of farmers and traders. A stop on the Hougang Heritage Trail, just off Upper Serangoon Road near Kovan.

    Look for Active mosque; visitors welcome outside prayer times

    2 Hillside Drive, Singapore 548920

  37. 37 Worth the detour within Upper Serangoon

    Lorong Halus Wetland (Serangoon Reservoir)

    An 18-football-field wetland on the Hougang/Defu edge — a former landfill transformed into a natural water-treatment site whose cattails bio-remediate rainwater before it enters the adjoining Serangoon Reservoir. Bounded by Kangkar to the west and Defu Industrial Park to the south, it's a family recreation spot reached over the red steel-railway-style Lorong Halus Bridge from Punggol Promenade.

    Look for Open daily, free; cycling, fishing decks & birdwatching

    Lorong Halus Wetland, Lorong Halus North (eastern bank of Serangoon Reservoir), Singapore

    Recommended by ,

    A Catholic parish on Kovan's western edge whose roots trace to 1959, when Fr Henri Saussard began ministering to the rubber tappers, fishermen and farmers of the Jalan Kayu area; the present church was blessed and opened at Christmas 1970. It continues to serve the north-eastern Catholic community around Serangoon Gardens and Kovan.

    Look for Active parish; Mass times on the church site

    301 Yio Chu Kang Road, Singapore 805910

    Recommended by ,

  67. 67 Deep cut within Upper Serangoon

    Holy Innocents' High School

    One of Singapore's first Chinese mission schools, founded in 1892 as Tao Nan School in the Upper Serangoon village and renamed Holy Innocents' Chinese Boys' School in 1920 under Fr Becheras. Part of Hougang's 'Holy Land' cluster of Catholic institutions around the Church of the Nativity; the school returned to a rebuilt Hougang campus, blessed by Archbishop Nicholas Chia in 2006.

    Look for Active school; grounds not open to visitors

    5 Lorong Low Koon, Singapore 536451

    Recommended by ,

  68. 68 Deep cut within Upper Serangoon

    Zi Yun Kai Ji Gong

    A Taoist temple complex completed in 1996 and a Hougang Heritage Trail 'Architectural Gems' landmark. It houses three older temples — Kai Hock Tong, Keat Sun Beo and Chao Ying Kong — relocated and consolidated from their original sites at Wolskel Road, Lorong Chuan and Yishun, a common Singapore story of temples resettled by redevelopment.

    Look for Active temple; open daytime

    56 Hougang Avenue 3, Singapore 538842

How we choose

Every place is recommended by named sources (Yelp and TripAdvisor never count as the recommender), pinned to its door from a published coordinate, and status-checked. Closed places stay, flagged, so you know they’re gone.

Must see
The places to plan a visit around — graded within each area, not across the city.
Worth the detour
Strong picks, worth going out of your way for.
Deep cut
For the curious: smaller, odder, more local.

Within each area, places are ordered by tier, then by number of named sources — never by popularity. Numbers on the cards match the pins on the map. No ratings, prices or opening hours are shown, because the guide doesn’t hold verified ones.
